props.title: Gettin' Square
props.initialSlug: Ex-con seeks redemption in Gold Coast crime world

sections.content: **Gettin' Square** (2003) stands as one of Australian cinema's sharpest crime comedies, following the tradition of darkly humorous Aussie films like **Two Hands** (1999) and **Chopper** (2000). David Wenham delivers a career-defining performance as Johnny "Spit" Spitieri, a heroin-addicted small-time criminal whose courtroom scene became instantly iconic in Australian film history. The film cleverly subverts typical crime thriller tropes while maintaining authentic Gold Coast atmosphere and criminal world dynamics that echo elements of **Animal Kingdom** (2010) but with a distinctly comedic edge.

sections.content: Director Jonathan Teplitzky crafts a distinctly Australian take on the crime genre, balancing humor with genuine tension in ways that influenced later films like **The Square** (2008) and **Son of a Gun** (2014). The Gold Coast setting provides a sun-drenched backdrop that contrasts beautifully with the dark undertones of the story, creating a unique aesthetic that differs from the typically gritty Melbourne or Sydney-based crime films of the era.

Sam Worthington's performance as Barry "Wattsy" Wirth represents some of his best pre-Hollywood work, showing the dramatic capabilities that would later land him roles in **Avatar** (2009). The film's exploration of redemption themes through both Wattsy and Spit's characters creates a compelling narrative that elevates it beyond simple crime comedy into something more nuanced and meaningful. sections.content: **Gettin' Square** emerged during a particularly strong period for Australian crime cinema, alongside films like **The Bank** (2001) and **Lantana** (2001). This era marked a shift toward more complex, character-driven crime narratives that balanced distinctly Australian humor with serious dramatic elements. The film's influence can be seen in later works like **The Square** (2008) and **Animal Kingdom** (2010), which similarly explore the intersection of crime, loyalty, and redemption in uniquely Australian contexts.
